learn.hook: Which sweet does your class love most? Don't guess. Collect the data and find out!
points: Data is a collection of facts, like numbers or names, gathered to answer a question.
Tally marks help us count as we collect: draw one stroke for each item, and make the fifth stroke cross the first four to make a bundle of 5.
A frequency table lists each item and how many times it appears (its frequency).
Arranging data in order, from smallest to largest, makes it easy to find the biggest and smallest values.
Check your total: the frequencies should add up to the number of things you counted.

example.q: Arjun asked 15 friends their favourite fruit: mango 7, banana 3, apple 5. Make tally marks and find the favourite.
steps: Mango: one bundle of 5 and 2 strokes = 7
example.answer: Mango is the favourite, chosen by 7 friends.

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers count which items sell most before Diwali, and cricket scorers keep data on every ball bowled.

games.title: Match the tally to the number
Data detectives
items: In tally marks, the fifth stroke is drawn across the first four.
This makes bundles of 5 that are easy to count.
A frequency table shows how many times each item appears.
Data can only be numbers, never words like 'mango'.
Names, colours and choices are data too.
A bundle of 5 and 2 more strokes stand for 7.
Sorting data from smallest to largest makes it harder to find the biggest value.
After sorting, the biggest value is simply at the end.

quiz.q: A tally shows 3 bundles of five and 2 single strokes. What number is this?
quiz.explain: Each bundle is 5, so 3 bundles make 15, and 2 more strokes make 17.
quiz.mistake: Writes the 3 and the 2 side by side (32) or forgets the single strokes

quiz.q: Meena asked her class how they come to school: Bus 12, Walk 8, Cycle 5, Car 3. How many children did she ask?
quiz.mistake: Forgets one group, or counts the number of groups (4)

quiz.q: Using Meena's data (Bus 12, Walk 8, Cycle 5, Car 3), how many more children come by bus than by cycle?
quiz.mistake: Adds the two numbers (17) instead of finding the difference

quiz.q: How do you show 14 using tally marks?
quiz.explain: 14 = 5 + 5 + 4, so it is 2 bundles of five and 4 single strokes.
quiz.mistake: Reads the digits 1 and 4 as 1 bundle and 4 strokes (which is only 9)

quiz.q: Scores in 6 cricket matches: 45, 12, 67, 30, 89, 54. Arrange them from smallest to largest. Which score is third?
quiz.explain: In order: 12, 30, 45, 54, 67, 89. The third score is 45.
quiz.mistake: Picks the third score from the unsorted list (67)

quiz.q: At a Makar Sankranti fair, Kabir counts 20 kites: red 6, yellow 4, green 3 and the rest blue. How many kites are blue?
quiz.explain: Red, yellow and green make 6 + 4 + 3 = 13. The rest: 20 − 13 = 7 blue kites.
quiz.mistake: Gives the total of the other colours (13) instead of what is left

quiz.q: What is the best way to find out the favourite sweet of the students in your class?
options: Ask every student and record the answers with tally marks
Count the sweets in a shop
quiz.explain: To answer a question about the class, collect data from everyone in the class and record it carefully.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one person's choice tells us about the whole class

quiz.q: In a frequency table of favourite colours, what does 'frequency' mean?
options: How many times each colour was chosen
The largest number in the table
The name of the person who chose it
quiz.explain: Frequency tells us how many times something appears in the data.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the item with how often it appears

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know which fruit all the birds like most: 'How do I collect and count everyone's answer?'
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! Ask everyone, tally as I go, then make a table. Now I know it's guava!
teach.nudge: Once I have everyone's answers, how do I keep count without getting muddled?

learn.hook: A picture is worth a thousand numbers! Graphs let you see data at a glance.
points: A pictograph shows data with pictures. A key tells what one picture stands for, like 1 🥭 = 4 mangoes.
Half a picture stands for half the key value.
A bar graph uses bars of the same width with equal gaps. The length of each bar shows the value.
A scale such as 1 unit = 10 children lets big numbers fit on the page. Choose a scale that keeps bars a sensible size.
Every graph needs a title and labels on both axes so readers know what it shows.

example.q: Key: 1 🥭 = 4 mangoes. A row shows 5 whole 🥭 and half a 🥭. How many mangoes?

learn.reallife: Newspapers show cricket run rates and rainfall with bar graphs, and school notice boards use pictographs for attendance.

items.text: Key: 1 🍦 = 5 ice creams. 35 ice creams need ___ pictures.
Scale: 1 unit = 10 km. A bar 4 units long shows ___ km.
In a bar graph, all bars should have the same ___.

quiz.q: In a pictograph, 1 🍪 = 10 cookies. Riya's row shows 4 🍪. How many cookies did she bake?
quiz.explain: Each picture means 10 cookies, so 4 pictures mean 4 × 10 = 40.
quiz.mistake: Counts the pictures without using the key (4) or adds 4 + 10

quiz.q: Key: 1 🚂 = 100 passengers. How many 🚂 pictures show 350 passengers?
quiz.explain: 300 passengers need 3 pictures and the extra 50 is half of 100, so half a picture: 3 and a half.
quiz.mistake: Drops the extra 50 (3) or rounds up (4)

quiz.q: A sweet shop sold laddoos in Diwali week: Mon 20, Tue 35, Wed 15, Thu 40. On which day were the most laddoos sold?
quiz.explain: 40 is the largest value, so Thursday has the longest bar.

quiz.q: Using the same laddoo data (Mon 20, Tue 35, Wed 15, Thu 40), how many laddoos were sold on Monday and Wednesday together?
Aisha's bar graph uses the scale 1 unit = 5 students. The bar for Kabaddi is 6 units long. How many students chose Kabaddi?
quiz.explain: Each unit stands for 5 students, so 6 units stand for 6 × 5 = 30 students.
quiz.mistake: Reads the bar length without the scale (6) or adds 6 + 5

quiz.q: Four baskets hold 120, 80, 200 and 150 mangoes. Which scale is best for a bar graph in your notebook?
quiz.explain: With 1 unit = 20, the bars are 6, 4, 10 and 7.5 units long: they fit and are easy to draw. 1 mango per unit makes bars far too long; 1000 makes them tiny; 7 gives awkward numbers.
quiz.mistake: Does not think about whether the bars will fit on the page

quiz.q: Key: 1 🌳 = 8 trees. How many trees does half a 🌳 show?
quiz.mistake: Treats half a picture as a whole picture (8) or doubles it (16)

quiz.q: Joseph's bar graph shows that Class 6A read 32 books and Class 6B read 24 books. How many more books did 6A read?
quiz.mistake: Adds the two values (56) instead of subtracting

teach.ask: Gappu sees a pictograph of mangoes: 'There are only 3 mango pictures. Does that mean 3 mangoes?'
teach.praise: Chirp! I must read the key first. If 1 picture means 10 mangoes, 3 pictures mean 30!
teach.nudge: Is there something on the graph that tells me what one picture is worth?
